title: Noel
full_review:
Christmas is often thought of as a season of hope and joy. But for many it is a time of loneliness and depression, a time when the sugarplum swirl of holly-jolly mirth only serves to magnify the sting of isolation and private pain.

It is this latter group -- the melancholic among the merry -- that populates the intertwined stories of "Noel" (Red Rose), a life-affirming holiday drama about faith, love and forgiveness.
Set in New York City, the movie marks the feature-film directorial debut of Chazz Palminteri, whose tough-guy persona in films like "A Bronx Tale" makes him an unlikely candidate to undertake such warmhearted fare. And though the film falls short of its Capraesque pretensions, Palminteri manages to strikes the right balance between the stories' sweet-and-sour elements, resulting in a feel-good potpourri that is sentimental without being schmaltzy, peopled by characters that seem real yet are not irredeemably cynical.

Those ripe for redemption include Rose (played by the always-watchable Susan Sarandon), a middle-aged divorcee, whose lack of yuletide cheer is rooted in personal tragedy and whose daily routine revolves around hospital visits to see her catatonic mother, and Mike (Paul Walker), a hotheaded cop whose uncontrollable jealous fits have driven a wedge between him and his beautiful fiancee, Nina (Penelope Cruz), who may or may not be pregnant with his child.

The other two New Yorkers destined for change by the end credits are Jules (Marcus Thomas), a young street hustler who goes to extremes to recapture the only happy Christmas experience he ever had, and Artie (Alan Arkin), a disturbed, guilt-ridden geezer haunted by his past.

The stories ultimately intersect on Christmas Eve. And while each has what you could call a "happy ending," the dovetailing denouements do not offer pat or quick-fix solutions to the characters' problems.

As in most films which consist of multiple story lines, some of the characters and plots in "Noel" are less fleshed out than others. The Jules character is the least interesting and gets somewhat lost in the narrative shuffle. The most engaging character, in part due to Sarandon's superior performance, is Rose.

Rose's fortunes are changed by a chance encounter with a stranger named Charlie (played by an unbilled Robin Williams), who intercedes at a pivotal moment in a scene echoing Frank Capra's "It's a Wonderful Life."

It turns out that -- for reasons left unexplained -- Charlie is a former priest who has forsaken his faith along with his collar. But just when Catholic viewers may start to say to themselves "here we go again," Palminteri shades in the character, revealing Charlie's soulful sadness over his spiritual emptiness.

Charlie realizes that he has lost something of profound value, a point underscored by his fingering of a small gold cross around his neck. Far from promoting a negative or cynical view of religious faith, the film affirms the importance of belief and prayer in our lives. It also conveys how God is found in other people and how he enters the loneliness of our hearts and tells us that we are loved (beautifully illustrated in a brief scene in which Rose reaches out to a patient whom no one visits).

The soundtrack features music by Academy Award-winning composer Alan Menken, as well as songs by the Daughters of St. Paul nuns' choir. The overall production feels modest and more like a made-for-TV movie than a theatrical feature, with Montreal standing in for New York for most of the exteriors. But the smallness of the film's scope is more than made up for by the largeness of its heart and by its edifying message -- summed up by the movie's tag line, "Miracles are closer than you think."

Due to an implied sexual encounter, some sexual comments and a few crude expressions, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
